skills.name: Identify careers and entrepreneurial opportunities in Creative Arts and Sports
skills.mastery: The child names careers in each area (visual arts: graphic designer, photographer, painter; physical education and sports: coach, referee, physiotherapist, athlete; music: musician, sound engineer, music teacher; theatre: actor, director, set designer), says what each does, and names entrepreneurial opportunities (selling crafts, event photography, a dance troupe, a sports academy, hiring out sound equipment). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G9.RUBRIC.1.1, CREA.G9.RUBRIC.1.2, CREA.G9.RUBRIC.1.3), never as a phone question: b) illustrate entrepreneurial opportunities in Creative Arts and Sports.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

prerequisites.reason: Earning a living is one of the roles of the arts and sport (Grade 8). Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.
The senior school pathways (Grade 9 Social Studies) include the Arts and Sports Science pathway these careers follow. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the only careers are performing ones (singer, athlete, actor).

example.question: Which is a career in Creative Arts and Sports?
example.correct_answer: many, such as a sound engineer, a referee or a set designer

misconceptions.cause: Performers are the people seen on TV.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "only being a famous singer" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List the people behind one concert or one match.
misconceptions.feedback: There are many careers behind the stage and the field, not only performers.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the arts and sport cannot earn a steady living.

example.question: Can a photographer earn a living?
example.wrong_answer: no, it is only a hobby
example.correct_answer: yes, at events, for businesses and in media

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard adults call the arts a hobby.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, it is only a hobby" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Count the paid jobs at one wedding: photographer, decorator, DJ, caterer.
misconceptions.feedback: Photographers and many other artists earn a living from their work.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts a physiotherapist under music.

example.question: Which area does a sports physiotherapist work in?
example.correct_answer: physical education and sports

misconceptions.cause: The child sorts by the word "therapy", not by the field.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "music" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: who does this person help, musicians or athletes?
misconceptions.feedback: A sports physiotherapist works in physical education and sports.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks entrepreneurship means only being employed by a company.

example.question: What is an entrepreneurial opportunity in Creative Arts?
example.correct_answer: starting your own business, such as selling crafts or event photography

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes having a job with starting a business.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "working for a big company" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare an employee with a learner who sells beadwork at a market.
misconceptions.feedback: An entrepreneur starts a business, such as selling crafts or hiring out a sound system.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Describe the elements of a play
skills.mastery: The child names the elements of a play (plot, characters, setting, theme, conflict, resolution, dialogue and stage directions) and says what each is in a short play they have read or watched. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

pick the right answer in a short story

The setting and order of a play (Grade 9 English) are read in the same term. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

skills.name: Tell power and reaction time from the other components of fitness
skills.mastery: The child says power is strength used quickly (a standing long jump, a vertical jump, a shot put) and reaction time is how fast the body responds to a signal (a sprint start, catching a dropped ruler), and picks an activity that trains each. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G9.RUBRIC.1.1, CREA.G9.RUBRIC.1.2, CREA.G9.RUBRIC.1.3), never as a phone question: b) perform activities demonstrating the components of fitness.

The full list of fitness components (Grade 7) includes these two. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

skills.name: Name pitches on the grand stave
skills.mastery: The child says the grand stave joins the treble and bass staves with a brace, names the lines and spaces of both (treble E G B D F and F A C E; bass G B D F A and A C E G), and places middle C on the ledger line between them. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

pick the right answer in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

prerequisites.reason: The bass staff (Grade 8) is the lower half of the grand stave. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.
The treble staff (Grade 7) is the upper half. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

skills.name: Group notes in four-four time with note extension
skills.mastery: The child says four-four time has four crotchet beats in a bar (beat 1 strong, beat 3 medium), that a dot adds half a note's value (dotted crotchet one and a half beats, dotted minim three) and a tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one sound, and checks that each bar adds up to four. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

prerequisites.reason: Grouping in three-four time and the dotted minim (Grade 8) come before four-four with note extension. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.
Adding halves and quarters (Grade 7 Maths) is how dotted notes and quavers fill a bar. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

skills.name: Build the scale of F major
skills.mastery: The child says F major has one flat, B flat, and its notes are F G A B-flat C D E F, starting and ending on F, and that the flat applies to every B in the piece. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Building G major with one sharp (Grade 8) is the same method for F major with one flat. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks conflict in a play means a physical fight.

example.question: What is conflict in a play?
example.correct_answer: the struggle or problem the characters face

misconceptions.cause: In daily speech conflict means fighting.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a fight with blows" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Find the conflict in a play with no fighting at all.
misconceptions.feedback: Conflict is the struggle or problem at the heart of the play, not only a fight.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says the resolution comes at the start of the play.

example.question: Where does the resolution come in a play?
example.correct_answer: near the end, when the conflict is settled

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes "resolution" with "introduction".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "at the start" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Order the parts of a known play: introduction, conflict, climax, resolution.
misconceptions.feedback: The resolution comes near the end, when the problem is settled.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the plot when asked for the theme.

example.question: What is the theme of a play?
example.correct_answer: the main idea it is about, such as honesty

misconceptions.cause: Retelling the events is easier than naming the idea.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "what happens first, then next" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask "what is the play teaching?" after retelling.
misconceptions.feedback: The theme is the main idea or lesson, not the events.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks stage directions are spoken by the actors.

example.question: Are stage directions spoken aloud in a performance?
example.correct_answer: no; they are acted, not spoken

misconceptions.cause: The child reads everything on the page as lines.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Act out "(she opens the door slowly)" without saying it.
misconceptions.feedback: Stage directions tell actors what to do. They are acted, not spoken.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks power is the same as strength.

example.question: What is the difference between strength and power?
example.correct_answer: power is strength used quickly

misconceptions.cause: Both words are used for strong people.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "they are the same" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare lifting a bag slowly (strength) and a vertical jump (power).
misconceptions.feedback: Power is strength used quickly, as in a jump.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks reaction time is how fast you run.

example.question: What is reaction time?
example.correct_answer: how quickly the body responds to a signal

misconceptions.cause: Both are about being quick.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "how fast you run" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Do the ruler-drop test: catch it as fast as you can.
misconceptions.feedback: Reaction time is how quickly you respond to a signal, not running speed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Picks a long jog as training for power.

example.question: Which activity trains power?
example.correct_answer: standing long jumps

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks any exercise builds every component.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a long, slow jog" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Match each activity to what it trains.
misconceptions.feedback: Explosive moves such as jumps train power. Long jogs train endurance.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a sprint start trains endurance.

example.question: A sprinter practises starts to the gun. What does this train?
example.correct_answer: reaction time

misconceptions.cause: The child links all running with endurance.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "endurance" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Practise starts to a clap and time the response.
misconceptions.feedback: Practising starts to a signal trains reaction time.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks there are two different middle Cs on the grand stave.

example.question: Is middle C on the treble staff the same note as middle C on the bass staff?
example.correct_answer: yes, the same note, written on a ledger line from either staff

misconceptions.cause: It is written in two places.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, they are different notes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Play middle C and show both ways of writing it.
misconceptions.feedback: Middle C is one note. It sits on a ledger line between the two staves.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Reads bass staff notes with the treble names.

example.question: What is the note on the bottom line of the bass staff?
example.correct_answer: G

misconceptions.cause: The treble names were learnt first and are used for both staves.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "E" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Check the clef before naming any note.
misconceptions.feedback: Bass staff lines are G B D F A. The bottom line is G.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the brace joins any two staves of different songs.

example.question: What does the brace on a grand stave show?
example.correct_answer: the two staves are played together as one part

misconceptions.cause: The child has not seen piano music.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "two different songs" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show piano music: both hands read at once.
misconceptions.feedback: The brace shows the two staves are read and played together.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the bass staff is for high notes.

example.question: Which staff of the grand stave holds the low notes?
example.correct_answer: the bass staff

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up "bass" and "treble".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the treble staff" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing low and point to the bass staff.
misconceptions.feedback: The bass staff holds the low notes; the treble staff the high ones.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a dot doubles a note's value.

example.question: How many beats is a dotted crotchet?
example.correct_answer: one and a half

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks the dot adds the whole note again.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "two" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: A crotchet is 1; half of 1 is a half; 1 + a half = one and a half.
misconceptions.feedback: A dot adds half the note's value. A dotted crotchet is one and a half beats.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Ties two notes of different pitch.

example.question: Can a tie join a C and a D?
example.correct_answer: no; a tie joins two notes of the same pitch

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes a tie with a slur.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a tie (same pitch, held) and a slur (different pitches, smooth).
misconceptions.feedback: A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer sound.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Writes a bar of four-four time with five beats.

example.question: A bar has a dotted minim and a minim. Is it a correct bar of four-four?
example.correct_answer: no; it has five beats

misconceptions.cause: The child adds notes by eye.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Write the beat count under each note.
misconceptions.feedback: A bar of four-four time holds exactly four beats.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Stresses every beat equally in four-four time.

example.question: Which beats are strong in four-four time?
example.correct_answer: beat 1 strongest, beat 3 medium

misconceptions.cause: The child counts evenly without stress.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "all four equally" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Count ONE two THREE four while stepping.
misconceptions.feedback: In four-four time beat 1 is strongest and beat 3 is medium.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts a sharp in F major.

example.question: F major has one...
example.correct_answer: flat

misconceptions.cause: G major, with one sharp, was learnt first.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "sharp" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Write F G A B C D E F and play it: B must be lowered.
misconceptions.feedback: F major has one flat, B flat.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Names E as the flat note in F major.

example.question: Which note is flat in F major?
example.correct_answer: B

misconceptions.cause: The child guesses the note before F.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "E" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Count the steps from F: the fourth note, B, is lowered.
misconceptions.feedback: In F major the B is flat.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Ends an F major scale on C.

example.question: On which note does F major start and end?
example.correct_answer: F

misconceptions.cause: C major feels like home from Grade 7.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "C" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: The key name is the home note.
misconceptions.feedback: F major starts and ends on F.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Flattens only the first B in a piece.

example.question: In F major, is every B played as B flat?
example.correct_answer: yes, every B

misconceptions.cause: The child treats the key signature like a one-time accidental.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "only the first one" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Circle every B in an F major tune.
misconceptions.feedback: The key signature makes every B a B flat.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Say what harmony or unity is in a picture and how it is made
skills.mastery: The child says harmony (unity) is when all the parts of a picture look as if they belong together, made by repeating similar colours, shapes, lines or textures, and tells it from contrast and dominance. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G9.RUBRIC.2.1, CREA.G9.RUBRIC.2.2, CREA.G9.RUBRIC.2.3), never as a phone question: d) paint a scenery composition to express harmony/unity.

pick the right answer in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

prerequisites.reason: Dominance (Grade 8) is the principle compared with harmony. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.
Balance (Grade 7) is another principle of arranging a picture. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

skills.name: Classify analogous colours on a colour wheel
skills.mastery: The child says analogous colours sit next to each other on the colour wheel (such as yellow, yellow-orange and orange, or blue, blue-green and green), give a calm, harmonious effect, and tells them from complementary colours, which sit opposite. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G9.RUBRIC.2.1, CREA.G9.RUBRIC.2.2, CREA.G9.RUBRIC.2.3), never as a phone question: c) illustrate a colour gradation strip for colour harmony.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

prerequisites.reason: Complementary colours (Grade 8) sit opposite; analogous ones sit beside each other. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.
The twelve-part colour wheel with tertiary colours (Grade 6) is where analogous colours are found. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks harmony means every part is exactly the same colour and shape.

example.question: Does harmony mean everything in a picture is identical?
example.correct_answer: no; parts are similar enough to belong together

misconceptions.cause: The child takes "unity" to mean sameness.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a landscape in greens and blues with varied shapes.
misconceptions.feedback: Harmony uses similar colours, shapes or lines, not identical ones.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Uses strong contrasting colours to show harmony.

example.question: Which colours give harmony: red and green, or yellow and orange?
example.correct_answer: yellow and orange

misconceptions.cause: Bright contrasts catch the eye, so the child thinks they work best.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "red and green" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Paint both pairs and ask which feels calm.
misconceptions.feedback: Neighbouring colours give harmony. Opposites give contrast.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says harmony is when one feature stands out.

example.question: A picture has one big bright feature that catches the eye. Which principle is that?
example.correct_answer: dominance

misconceptions.cause: Both are principles learnt in Grades 8 and 9.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "harmony" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: does one thing stand out, or does everything belong together?
misconceptions.feedback: One feature standing out is dominance. Everything belonging together is harmony.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks repeating shapes in a picture is boring and should be avoided.

example.question: How can an artist create unity in a picture?
example.correct_answer: repeat similar shapes, colours or lines

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks variety is always better.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "never repeat any shape" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Find repeated shapes in a woven mat.
misconceptions.feedback: Repeating similar shapes, colours or lines creates unity.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says analogous colours sit opposite each other on the wheel.

example.question: Where are analogous colours on the colour wheel?
example.correct_answer: next to each other

misconceptions.cause: Grade 8 complementary colours were opposite, so the child keeps that rule.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "opposite each other" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Point at three neighbours on the wheel.
misconceptions.feedback: Analogous colours are neighbours. Complementary colours are opposite.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Picks blue and orange as analogous.

example.question: Which group is analogous?
example.correct_answer: blue, blue-green and green

misconceptions.cause: The child remembers blue and orange as a pair from Grade 8.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "blue and orange" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Find each colour on the wheel and check if they touch.
misconceptions.feedback: Blue, blue-green and green are neighbours, so they are analogous.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks any three colours are analogous.

example.question: Are red, yellow and blue analogous?
example.correct_answer: no; they are the primaries, spread apart on the wheel

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks "analogous" means a group of three.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Mark red, yellow and blue on the wheel: they are far apart.
misconceptions.feedback: Analogous colours must sit side by side on the wheel.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks analogous colours give a loud, clashing effect.

example.question: What effect do analogous colours usually give?
example.correct_answer: calm and harmonious

misconceptions.cause: Bright paint looks loud to the child whatever its neighbours.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "loud and clashing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare an analogous strip with a complementary strip.
misconceptions.feedback: Analogous colours blend smoothly and give a calm effect.

misconceptions.error: Sounds both notes of a tie separately.

example.question: How many times do you sound two tied notes?

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "twice" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Clap a tied pair as one long clap.
misconceptions.feedback: Tied notes are sounded once and held for both values.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a dot after a note means a short silence.

example.correct_answer: makes the note longer by half its value

misconceptions.cause: The dot looks like a small rest.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "adds a short silence" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Clap a crotchet, then a dotted crotchet; hear it held longer.
misconceptions.feedback: A dot makes the note half as long again, not a silence.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks note extension does not change the feel of a rhythm.

example.question: Does adding dots change how a rhythm feels?

misconceptions.cause: The child counts beats but does not listen to the feel.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Clap a plain and a dotted version of one bar.
misconceptions.feedback: Dots and ties give long-short patterns and change the feel.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Lands the hop on the other foot.

example.question: In the triple jump, which foot does the hop land on?
example.correct_answer: the same foot you took off from

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks every phase changes feet.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the other foot" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Chalk the pattern: right, right, left, both (for a right-foot take-off).
misconceptions.feedback: The hop lands on the take-off foot; the step lands on the other foot.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts the phases in the order jump, step, hop.

example.question: What is the order of the triple jump phases?
example.correct_answer: hop, step, jump

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the three words but not their order.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "jump, step, hop" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say "hop, step, jump" while walking through it.
misconceptions.feedback: The order is hop, step, then jump into the pit.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Makes the hop as big as possible and has no energy left for the jump.

example.question: Should the hop be as big as possible?
example.correct_answer: no; the three phases should be balanced

misconceptions.cause: The first phase feels like the most important.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, the bigger the better" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Measure three jumps: one with a huge hop, one balanced.
misconceptions.feedback: Balance the hop, step and jump so you keep speed for all three.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Measures the triple jump from where the jump phase starts.

example.question: Where is a triple jump measured from?
example.wrong_answer: from where the last jump starts
example.correct_answer: from the take-off board to the nearest mark in the pit

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the last jump into the pit as the jump.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "from where the last jump starts" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Lay a tape from the board to the pit.
misconceptions.feedback: The whole distance from the take-off board to the nearest mark in the pit is measured.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Names the 800 m as a long distance race.

example.question: Which is a long distance race?

misconceptions.cause: The 800 m feels long to a learner.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "800 m" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.feedback: The 800 m is middle distance. 5 000 m, 10 000 m and the marathon are long distance.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Starts a long race at sprint speed.

example.question: How should a long distance race be started?
example.correct_answer: at an even pace you can keep

misconceptions.cause: Sprint starts were learnt first.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "as fast as possible" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Run two laps flat out from the start and two at even pace; compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Start at an even pace you can keep for the whole race.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Uses long bounding strides in a long race.

example.question: Which stride suits a long distance race?
example.correct_answer: a short, relaxed, economical stride

misconceptions.cause: Long strides look fast.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "long bounding strides" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Run 400 m bounding, then with short relaxed strides.
misconceptions.feedback: A short relaxed stride saves energy over a long race.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a runner should not drink water during a long race.

example.question: Should runners drink water in a long race?
example.correct_answer: yes, small sips at water points

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, it slows them" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.feedback: A mosaic is made of small pieces of material, not paint dots.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.feedback: A mosaic usually uses one kind of material in different colours.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a small amount of a banned drug is acceptable.

example.question: Is a small amount of a banned substance allowed?
example.correct_answer: no; any banned substance is doping

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks only large amounts count.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, if it is small" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Read an anti-doping rule together.
misconceptions.feedback: Any banned substance is doping and is not allowed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks lying about age to play in a younger group is harmless.

example.question: Is it fair to lie about age to play in a younger team?
example.wrong_answer: yes, it helps the team win
example.correct_answer: no; it is cheating and unfair to younger players

misconceptions.cause: The child focuses on winning.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, it helps the team win" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Discuss how the younger players feel.
misconceptions.feedback: Lying about age is cheating and unfair to others.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks losing a match on purpose for money is a private choice.

example.question: A player is paid to lose a match on purpose. Is that ethical?
example.correct_answer: no; it is match fixing and cheats everyone

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the choice as affecting only the player.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, it is their choice" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Talk about fans, team mates and the sport.
misconceptions.feedback: Losing on purpose for money is match fixing. It cheats everyone.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks doping is banned only because it is unhealthy.

example.question: Give two reasons why doping is banned.
example.correct_answer: it is cheating, and it harms health

misconceptions.cause: Health warnings are what the child has heard.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "only because it is unhealthy" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Discuss what doping does to fairness.
misconceptions.feedback: Doping is banned because it is cheating and because it harms health.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Starts a critique by judging before describing.

example.question: What is the first step of a critique?
example.wrong_answer: say if it is good or bad
example.correct_answer: describe what you see

misconceptions.cause: Judging is the quickest response.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "say if it is good or bad" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Use the four steps: describe, analyse, interpret, judge.
misconceptions.feedback: Start by describing what you see. Judge last.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Judges an artwork without giving reasons.

example.question: Which is a good critique judgement?
example.correct_answer: it works because the warm colours draw the eye to the dancer

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks an opinion is enough.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "it is bad" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Add "because" to every judgement.
misconceptions.feedback: Give a reason from the work for every judgement.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Comments on the artist as a person instead of the work.

example.question: What should a critique comment on?
example.wrong_answer: whether the artist is a nice person
example.correct_answer: the artwork itself

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the artist and mixes the two.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "whether the artist is a nice person" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Cover the name and critique the work only.
misconceptions.feedback: A critique is about the artwork, not the artist as a person.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives a description when asked for the meaning.

example.question: What is the interpretation step of a critique?
example.wrong_answer: listing what is in the picture
example.correct_answer: saying what the work means or expresses

misconceptions.cause: Describing is easier than interpreting.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "listing what is in the picture" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask "what is the artist telling us?" after describing.
misconceptions.feedback: Interpretation says what the work means, not only what is in it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
